Package org.apache.juneau.commons.beanquery

Enum Class SearchType

java.lang.Object
java.lang.Enum<SearchType>
org.apache.juneau.commons.beanquery.SearchType
All Implemented Interfaces:
Serializable, Comparable<SearchType>, Constable
public enum SearchType extends Enum<SearchType>
The per-column value type that governs which search operators apply to a column and how a bare (no leading $) pattern token is interpreted.

A column's value type selects both the operator set offered for that column (SearchOperatorSet.forType(SearchType)) and the leaf-comparison semantics a context applies. The lowercase wire token is the stable external spelling. bareHelp() is a fixed, one-sentence explanation of bare-token behavior intended for display in a search-bar popover.

Bare-token behavior per type:
  • TEXT / ID — case-insensitive substring (same idea as $contains).
  • VERSION — dotted-tuple prefix.
  • NUMERIC / TIMESTAMP / ENUM / BOOLEAN — exact equality.
Example:

String help = SearchType.VERSION.bareHelp(); // help == "Matches any version starting with this prefix, e.g. 250 matches 250.1 and 250.2.3."

Example (typing a literal):

// Type a literal the same way for every engine, so a bad value is BAD_VALUE (400) everywhere. Object v = SearchType.NUMERIC.parse("42"); // BigDecimal("42")

Since:
10.0.0

  • Enum Constant Details

    • TEXT

      public static final SearchType TEXT
      Free text. Bare token is a case-insensitive substring match.

    • ID

      public static final SearchType ID
      An id-like string (identifiers, keys). Bare token is a case-insensitive substring match, same as TEXT.

    • NUMERIC

      public static final SearchType NUMERIC
      A number. Bare token is exact equality; supports the ordered operators.

    • VERSION

      public static final SearchType VERSION
      A dotted version tuple (e.g. 10.0.0). Bare token is a dotted-tuple prefix; supports the ordered operators and $prefix.

    • TIMESTAMP

      public static final SearchType TIMESTAMP
      An instant/timestamp. Bare token is exact equality; supports the ordered operators.

      Offset advice: a value with an explicit offset (2026-09-30T12:00:00Z, 2026-09-30T12:00:00-04:00) always denotes one absolute instant. The local forms (a date-time without an offset, or a bare date) have no zone: in-memory matching treats them as UTC, while a SQL engine hands them to the database, which interprets them in the session time zone. The two can therefore disagree, so prefer the offset forms (or epoch milliseconds, which are always UTC) in any search that must behave identically everywhere. See parse(String).

    • ENUM

      public static final SearchType ENUM
      A one-of enumerated value. Bare token is a case-insensitive exact match.

    • BOOLEAN

      public static final SearchType BOOLEAN
      A boolean. Bare token is exact equality; supports only $eq/$ne.

    • parse

      public Object parse(String value)
      Parses a decoded literal (quotes stripped, escapes undone) into this type's Java representation.

      NUMERIC parses to BigDecimal; BOOLEAN to Boolean (case-insensitive true/false); TIMESTAMP to OffsetDateTime (has an offset), LocalDateTime (no offset), LocalDate (date only), or, for a bare integer, an OffsetDateTime at UTC built from epoch milliseconds (optional leading -; no +). The local forms carry no zone - see the offset advice on TIMESTAMP. TEXT, ID, ENUM and VERSION are returned unchanged (never null; a null value becomes "").

      Example:

      BigDecimal n = (BigDecimal)SearchType.NUMERIC.parse("-3.5");

      Parameters:
      value - The decoded literal text, or null (treated as empty).
      Returns:
      The parsed value.
      Throws:
      BeanQuerySyntaxException - (code BAD_VALUE) If value does not parse for this type (NUMERIC, BOOLEAN or TIMESTAMP only).
      Since:
      10.0.0

    • parse

      public Object parse(String value, Instant requestTime)
      Parses a decoded literal like parse(String), resolving a relative-duration literal against requestTime instead of the current instant.

      A relative-duration literal is [+-]<n>(ms|s|m|h|d) (lowercase units only), e.g. -24h, or a signed ISO-8601 duration (PT24H, -PT24H, +PT30M, P1D) with identical semantics (only one leading sign; PT-1H, years, months and weeks are BAD_VALUE). For NUMERIC it parses to the signed amount in milliseconds (a BigDecimal; "now" is never involved). For TIMESTAMP it parses to requestTime plus the signed amount, as an OffsetDateTime at UTC. A bare signed number such as -5 is never a duration, and a total that overflows a long (for TIMESTAMP, after adding requestTime's epoch milliseconds) is BAD_VALUE. On BOOLEAN a duration is BAD_VALUE; TEXT, ID, ENUM and VERSION are untyped and keep the text literally. Every other literal shape parses exactly as in parse(String); parse(String) itself delegates here with Instant.now().

      Example:

      Instant now = Instant.parse("2026-09-30T12:00:00Z"); Object yesterday = SearchType.TIMESTAMP.parse("-24h", now); // 2026-09-29T12:00Z Object ms = SearchType.NUMERIC.parse("-24h", now); // BigDecimal("-86400000")

      Parameters:
      value - The decoded literal text, or null (treated as empty).
      requestTime - The instant a relative-duration TIMESTAMP literal resolves against. Must not be null.
      Returns:
      The parsed value.
      Throws:
      BeanQuerySyntaxException - (code BAD_VALUE) If value does not parse for this type (NUMERIC, BOOLEAN or TIMESTAMP only).
      Since:
      10.0.0
